pr_title: JsonSerializer.DeserializeAsyncEnumerable should not wait until buffer is filled.
pr_body:
From https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/70107#issuecomment-1148808314. The current implementation of the [internal `ReadFromStreamAsync` method](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/da79dc611cba819dce6da3966dc4c7503524fa18/src/libraries/System.Text.Json/src/System/Text/Json/Serialization/JsonSerializer.Read.Stream.cs#L525-L560) will keep reading from the stream until either the internal buffer is filled or the stream EOF's, which is intended as a performance optimization to avoid redundant deserialization calls. While this makes sense in the case of `DeserializeAsync`, it can impact liveness when deserializing IAsyncEnumerable sequences in examples such as the one seen in #70107.

This PR changes the behavior of stream reading specifically in `DeserializeAsyncEnumerable` such that the deserializer is invoked as soon as the first `Stream.ReadAsync` operation returns. Moreover it makes a few more changes:

* Encapsulate the buffer management logic behind the `ReadBufferState` struct.
* Avoid allocating a new JsonTypeInfo instance on every IAsyncEnumerator initialization.

Fix #70107.

issue_context.title: [System.Text.Json] DeserializeAsyncEnumerable is delayed emitting objects when writing asynchronously to stream
comments:
The root cause of this behavior is the current implementation of the [internal `ReadFromStreamAsync` method](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/da79dc611cba819dce6da3966dc4c7503524fa18/src/libraries/System.Text.Json/src/System/Text/Json/Serialization/JsonSerializer.Read.Stream.cs#L525-L560). The method will keep reading from the stream until either the internal buffer is filled or the stream EOF's: this was intended as a performance optimization to avoid redundant partial deserialization passes, but it is clear that it could impact liveness specifically for the case of `DeserializeAsyncEnumerable`.

We could try tweaking this method slightly specifically for `DeserializeAsyncMethod`, possibly trading off deserialization performance for decreased delays in element reads.

review_comments: I think this variable is mis-named. I'd rename it to something like "_endOfInput"
(i.e. first block can also be the last one but you don't know until you're done reading)

It denotes that we've read the final chunk of UTF-8 data to be fed into the deserializer. The deserializer itself accesses the `IsFinalBlock` property to determine if it has finished. The name predates this change and I think it's appropriate.
Why not just make this method static?
It can be, but wrote it like this for symmetry with the sync variant. It doesn't change the amount of copying needed in any case.
Can this use the new Stream.ReadAtLeastAsync method when targeting .NET 7 and fillBuffer is true?  And if fillBuffer is false, why even call this method rather than just calling ReadAsync directly?

> Can this use the new Stream.ReadAtLeastAsync method when targeting .NET 7 and fillBuffer is true?

It could, but we still need to polyfill for all the other TFMs. Does it make a difference perf-wise?

> And if fillBuffer is false, why even call this method rather than just calling ReadAsync directly?

The method does a bit of added bookkeeping like skipping BOM bytes and tracking the maximum watermark in the rented buffers.

> Does it make a difference perf-wise?

No. It'd just be nice to use the built-in functionality where it exists. We could implement the same method as an extension polyfill for downlevel.

> The method does a bit of added bookkeeping like skipping BOM bytes and tracking the maximum watermark in the rented buffers.

But it's also more expensive: if the stream.ReadAsync call completes asynchronously, it'll force this extra level of async method to suspend and allocate.

> > Does it make a difference perf-wise?
> 
> No. It'd just be nice to use the built-in functionality where it exists. We could implement the same method as an extension polyfill for downlevel.

I gave it a shot, but honestly I don't feel like it's improving the codebase. Netstandard2.0 doesn't have `Stream.ReadAsync` overloads that accept `Memory<T>` so you can't really polyfill the exact `ReadAtLeastAsync` method signature (`ArraySegment<byte>` seeming like the next best thing), so it all becomes messier than necessary.
isn't it better to keep count/length in the locals in the loop and then assign them back once you're done?
Ultimately this will compile into an async state machine so any locals will be represented using fields in the SM struct.
considering you return the copy of this buffer state in some of the methods is it safe to do it like this? Should you add some guarding against double free?

I'm seeing you always assign back the copy of the struct, please make sure to at least add comment on the method returning copy and the class itself. Alternative perhaps some `#if DEBUG` with extra code protecting us against this pattern (i.e. wrap buffer in ref type, set it to null on Dispose and check with Debug.Assert)

> considering you return the copy of this buffer state in some of the methods is it safe to do it like this? Should you add some guarding against double free?

Yes, assuming you somehow end up disposing two copies of the same struct then that is a possibility, but we're not doing this in the handful of methods that creates the struct. 

> perhaps some #if DEBUG extra code protecting us against this pattern (i.e. wrap buffer in ref type, set it to null on Dispose and check with Debug.Assert)

Can you give an example? Not sure I understand. FWIW this is not new code, I'm just moving existing logic to the struct.
I understand the condition, my question is what assert could guard against such a potential scenario.
as per discussion offline, better to do this for all similar structs in separate PR in order to potentially find potential memory corruption bug
rather than keeping variable and special code, would it make sense to simply handle this separately (i.e. separate call in the beginning)
Not sure I follow, this handling needs to happen after the first read.
I was thinking about separate read but I don't really have strong preference or data telling if one way or the other is faster
